metadata.title: DC public schools face special grand jury probe into attendance, truancy and graduation records

sources.news_title: Prosecutors are questioning school staff and reviewing data as preliminary figures show 50.4% of D.C. students in grades 9-12 were chronically truant.
sources.text:
Federal prosecutors have launched a rare special grand jury probe into D.C. public schools, zeroing in on truancy, graduation rates and attendance records.
The investigation, which was first reported by The Washington Post, is examining the supervision and oversight of young people in the nation’s capital, according to people familiar with the matter.
D.C. public schools have been contacted about truancy and graduation rates, as well as attendance records. One law enforcement official emphasized this probe is about, "safeguarding youth in the District."
The use of a special grand jury is unusual. Fox News is told a judge must approve the creation of such a panel, which can conduct a sweeping investigation and issue a detailed report on its findings even if prosecutors ultimately file no criminal charges.
DETROIT SCHOOLS OFFER STUDENTS UP TO $1,000 FOR PERFECT ATTENDANCE AS PROGRAM EXPANDS
A spokesperson for U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office told the Washington Post it could neither confirm nor deny an investigation.
The office of D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser said its focus remains on the new school year.
"Our focus remains on welcoming students and families back for a strong start to the new school year, and that is what we want our principals and teachers focused on as well," the mayor’s office told the Washington Post. "We make all school data public and will continue to do so."
The Washington Post reported that senior prosecutor Steven Vandervelden, one of Pirro’s top allies in the U.S. attorney’s office, is overseeing the inquiry.
Pirro has repeatedly linked school truancy to youth crime and disruptive teen gatherings in the District. At a May news conference, she said authorities could take action when teens repeatedly break curfew or skip school.
GRADY JUDD PUTS PARENTS ON NOTICE OVER TIKTOK TEEN TAKEOVERS: 'WE'RE GONNA COME LOCK YOU UP TOO'
"We’re coming for you, and we’re coming for your parents," Pirro said.
She also said her office wanted school records involving students accused of chronic truancy and curfew violations, according to the Washington Post. The outlet reported that the city did not voluntarily turn over those records.
The new probe comes years after D.C. schools were rocked by a graduation scandal centered on Ballou High School. A 2018 city investigation found the school had awarded diplomas to students who failed to satisfy attendance rules or had improperly completed makeup coursework.
While the scandal initially centered on Ballou High School, it eventually spread to several D.C. high schools. The investigation found that about one-third of D.C. students who graduated in 2017 had not actually met the requirements for a diploma, according to the Washington Post. District officials later said they tightened enforcement of attendance standards.
MORE THAN 400K NEW YORK CITY CHILDREN ENROLLED IN FAILING PUBLIC SCHOOLS: REPORT
Absenteeism, however, has persisted. During the 2023-24 school year, nearly 16,000 D.C. Public Schools students, roughly one-third of K-12 enrollment, were considered truant after missing at least two weeks of classes without an excuse, the Washington Post reported last year.
The special grand jury’s work is unfolding as D.C.’s school system, which serves more than 50,000 students, begins a new academic year.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Office of the State Superintendent of Education for comment.

Federal grand jury investigation puts new focus on DC school attendance
WASHINGTON (7News) — A federal grand jury investigation is putting new focus on attendance, truancy and graduation records inside D.C. Public Schools (DCPS) as 7News finds striking differences in how often students are showing up across the District.
Sources told 7News federal prosecutors have contacted and questioned DCPS teachers and other school personnel about truancy, graduation rates and how attendance records are kept. Some of those employees are connected to Ballou High School.
The investigation comes as 7News reviewed the latest attendance data from the D.C. Office of the State Superintendent of Education, or OSSE.
RELATED | DC schools see gains in math and reading, but attendance remains a concern
Preliminary data for the 2025 to 2026 school year shows 50.4% of D.C. students in grades nine through 12 are chronically truant.
OSSE told 7News that the number includes students attending both traditional public schools and public charter schools. The agency said its preliminary chronic truancy figures reflect students who missed 10% or more of the school year without an excused reason.
The high school number stands out because students in younger grades moved in the opposite direction.
Citywide, chronic truancy fell from 36.6% during the 2024 to 2025 school year to 35.5% in 2025 to 2026.
Among students in kindergarten through second grade, the rate fell from 30.6% to 28%. For grades three through five, it dropped from 30.4% to 29%, and for grades six through eight it declined from 36.4% to 34.7%.
But among students in grades nine through 12, chronic truancy increased from 49.3% to 50.4%.
Chronic absenteeism is also particularly high among older students. OSSE data shows 57% of students in grades nine through 12 were chronically absent during the latest school year, meaning they missed at least 10% of their enrolled school days for any reason.
The school-by-school numbers show an even wider range.
At Ballou High School, 84.4% of students were chronically truant during the 2025 to 2026 school year, up from 83.3% the year before.
That means more than eight in 10 students at Ballou met the chronic truancy threshold.
Ballou is not alone. Preliminary OSSE data shows Anacostia High School had a chronic truancy rate of 84.1%, Dunbar High School 79.6%, Eastern High School 78.5%, H.D. Woodson High School 77.6%, and Roosevelt High School 72.7%.
But some D.C. high schools have dramatically lower rates. School Without Walls High School recorded a chronic truancy rate of 2.3%, while Benjamin Banneker High School was at 8%.
The differences are significant because they show the attendance problem is not playing out the same way at every school.
Hedy Chang, founder of Attendance Works and a national expert on student attendance, told 7News the numbers of any kid missing school should concern families and education leaders.
“Absolutely. And they should be concerned,” Chang said, calling for an “all hands on deck approach” focused on making sure students are engaged in school, see school as something worth showing up to and receive help overcoming barriers that may keep them from attending.
Chang said there is no single explanation for why students miss large amounts of school.
She said schools need to understand whether students are facing barriers, whether they feel disconnected from school and whether they believe what they are learning is meaningful.
“School climate matters more than ever,” Chang said.
She said schools should look at whether students have an adult they connect with, relationships with peers, opportunities that keep them engaged and a sense that they belong.
Chang said those questions can become particularly important for older students.
“Kids don’t feel so engaged by school,” Chang said. “They wonder what’s the point, you know, how does this relate to my future?”
She said improving attendance can require several approaches at once, including stronger family engagement, improving students’ connection to school, making learning more relevant, addressing health and safety issues and removing barriers such as transportation and access to technology.
Chang also said extremely high levels of missed school can signal a problem larger than any one student or family.
“I suspect you have some systemic issues going on when you have such high levels of kids being chronically absent,” Chang said.
She said missed class time can also create problems that build on themselves.
“If you miss a lot of school, it makes it harder to learn how to read,” Chang said. “If you don’t have the literacy skills you need, it makes school less interesting and you don’t wanna show up as much. So these are intertwined issues.”
D.C. education leaders have also acknowledged attendance remains a major challenge.
At a briefing around the start of the school year, before news of the federal grand jury investigation became public, a District education official said chronic absenteeism and chronic truancy remain significant concerns.
“We know that if students are not in school, we can’t teach them, we can’t reach them,” the official said.
District education leaders also specifically acknowledged the challenge among older students, saying there is more work to do at the high school level.
They pointed to school climate and culture, as well as whether students are interested and engaged in the courses they are taking.
Interim DCPS Chancellor Kim Jackson separately described chronic absenteeism as one of the school system’s greatest challenges and said improving attendance is a top priority.
Jackson said DCPS is working with schools and communities to support students, including through community schools and hubs that can help families address issues such as health care and school uniforms that could create barriers to attendance.
OSSE told 7News it is working with DCPS, public charter schools and community organizations to address absenteeism and chronic truancy through attendance data, school supports and its attendance dashboard.
The agency said chronic truancy can put students at greater risk of falling behind academically, not graduating on time and facing longer-term challenges.
OSSE also pointed to a recent report from the Deputy Mayor for Education and EveryDay Labs that found D.C. attendance has improved by nine percentage points since its pandemic peak and is outpacing most peer cities in attendance recovery.
The agency said there is still “significant work ahead” and that it remains focused on reducing barriers to attendance and improving student engagement.
Graduation data adds another layer to the questions now surrounding D.C. schools.
At Ballou, 136 of 153 students in the 2025 graduating cohort graduated, an 88.9% graduation rate. The year before, 100 of 128 students graduated, a rate of 78.1%.
That is an increase of more than 10 percentage points in one year.
Those numbers should not be directly compared to Ballou’s chronic truancy rate as though they describe the same students. Attendance and graduation data measure different populations, and the available data does not show whether the students classified as chronically truant were the same students who ultimately received diplomas.
The relationship between attendance and graduation requirements has drawn scrutiny at Ballou before.
A city investigation in 2018 found Ballou graduated students who missed too many classes or improperly completed makeup courses. The controversy later expanded beyond Ballou, and a broader review found about one-third of D.C.’s 2017 graduating class did not meet graduation requirements.
The FBI also investigated the earlier controversy, though that probe did not appear to result in charges. The city later said it strengthened enforcement of its attendance requirements.
The Washington Post first reported federal prosecutors had convened a rarely used special grand jury focused on D.C. youth that includes an examination of public schools. According to the Post, the broader inquiry appears to include questions about the supervision and oversight of children in the District.
Special grand juries are unusual. Unlike a typical grand jury, a special grand jury can, with a judge’s approval, issue a report detailing its findings even if prosecutors ultimately do not bring criminal charges.
The existence of the investigation does not establish wrongdoing by DCPS, Ballou, school employees or any other individual. The exact scope and potential outcome of the federal inquiry remain unclear.
7News asked Chang whether a broader investigation into school attendance could help identify solutions.
“I think it depends on how you carry that investigation out,” Chang said.
She said any review should continue asking why students are missing school but should also identify schools, teachers and programs where attendance has improved.
“That often can give you insights into what can be scaled,” Chang said.
That point is particularly notable given the wide differences in attendance rates among D.C. high schools, with some schools reporting chronic truancy rates above 80% while others remain in the single digits.
Mayor Muriel Bowser’s office provided the following statement to 7News:
“Our focus remains on welcoming students and families back for a strong start to the new school year, and that is what we want our principals and teachers focused on as well. We make all school data public and will continue to do so.”
7News also asked whether the mayor had a statement specifically regarding the federal grand jury investigation. Her office did not directly answer that question.
7News has also reached out to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for more information about the investigation.

- Outer beauty: Advisory Neighborhood Commission 1E is inviting residents to join community members for Neighborhood Beautification Day tomorrow at Bruce Monroe Park. Volunteers will pick up litter, weed, clean, plant, mulch, and improve neighborhood tree boxes—and perhaps even adopt tree boxes—along Georgia Avenue NW. “We want everyone who cares about the neighborhood to feel welcome to pitch in,” says event organizer ANC 1E Vice Chair Audra Grant. No experience necessary. Plus one point for public service. +1 [ANC 1E]
- Tech no: As part of a nationwide campaign called Purge Palantir, patients, activists, and nurses from National Nurses United showed up at Palantir’s D.C. headquarters yesterday to demand hospitals and elected officials cut ties with the AI company. Palantir’s ELITE app identifies people for arrest using improperly obtained Medicaid data. “No part of the country has been untouched by the terror and violence of ICE and CBP, enabled by Palantir’s technology. … We have to resist a future where tech billionaires control our politics and our public resources,” says NNU President Jamie Brown, RN. Plus one point for protesting but minus one point for surveillance. 0 [NUN]

Now she has convened a special grand jury to look into D.C. Public Schools regarding student supervision, truancy, and violence. Prosecutors have called DCPS teachers and personnel to appear and answer questions about truancy, graduation rates, and attendance records. “We’re coming for you, and we’re coming for your parents,” said Cruella De Vil, I mean Pirro. Minus two points for federal overreach and harassment. -2 [Post]
- Wage war: Research from the Institute for Policy Studies suggests CEOs at the 100 lowest-paying corporations in the U.S. earned 614 times more than their workers in 2025. Between 2019 and 2025, CEO pay increased 41.4 percent, twice as much as the median worker pay increase. Average CEO pay at low-wage 100 corporations was $17.5 million last year, compared with median worker pay of $36,571. Many employees at these companies also rely on Medicaid and SNAP. Minus two points for low pay and greedy bosses. -2 [Guardian]
- We object: Organizations that assist those who want to leave the military as conscientious objectors over U.S. military strikes on alleged drug boats and Iran war targets are seeing an uptick in applications. One group has seen six times as many applicants as it typically sees, currently at 140. To be a conscientious objector, one must have a “firm, fixed, sincere and deeply held” moral, religious, or ethical belief that opposes participation in war. Troops are concerned that they are being asked to violate international law, and the U.S. military may be targeting civilian infrastructure. One told MS Now, “When you volunteer to sign up for the military, despite what some people might think, you’re not signing up to be a robot.” Plus one point for a moral compass but minus one for the state of our military. 0 [MS Now]

In her continuing quest to figure out how to cling to a job that she doesn’t deserve, U.S. Attorney for Washington, D.C., Jeanine Pirro spun up a special grand jury earlier this month—something that is uncommon in D.C., with a population of just around 700,000.
Special grand juries are generally for jurisdictions of more than 4 million people, and they’re also supposed to be used for things like lengthy investigations into organized crime and public corruption.
But Pirro seems to be using hers to harass public schools.
It’s honestly astonishing how much capacity this administration has for stupid garbage like this. It’s like the special grand jury equivalent of the misuse of plain vanilla grand juries to facilitate vindictive prosecutions against President Donald Trump’s perceived enemies.
So Pirro is apparently taking a break from drinking boxed wine to investigate the supervision and oversight of kids in D.C. public schools.
Now, we’re not talking about things like whether schools are keeping children safe from sexual assault or physical harm. We know full well this administration doesn’t care about that, and instead has a whole-of-government effort to cover up Trump’s connection to pedophile pal Jeffrey Epstein.
No, this is over graduation, truancy rates, and attendance records.
Wait, what?
Related | Jeanine Pirro just can’t stop losing
D.C. is the only place, really, where the Justice Department can get its grubby, evil little mitts on this sort of thing, thanks to the unfortunate liminal situation of not being a state and therefore falling under federal control. It’s basically the same reason that allows other states’ National Guards to stay in D.C. indefinitely. So its schools have now fallen under Pirro’s gimlet eye.
Oh, sorry. That apparently means “a piercing or watchful eye,” not “an eye filled to the brim with gimlets.” We regret the error.
There’s no doubt that this special grand jury exists to safeguard Pirro’s job, not, as some random law enforcement official told the Washington Post, “about safeguarding youth.”
What this is really about is further harassing a blue city that hates Trump and lending credence to his unhinged, unfounded belief that D.C. was a nightmarish murder hellhole before him.
In service of this, Pirro has used her role to seek to prosecute 12-year-olds as adults. Well, that’s one way to juice her stats.
And in case you weren’t clear, Pirro screamed the quiet part out loud in a red wine-fueled screed. She literally wants to make arrests “when teens are repeatedly violating the curfew, when they are repeatedly truant from school.”
“We’re coming for you, and we’re coming for your parents,” she added.
Great.
More evidence that this whole effort is risible bullshit is that it’s in the hands of the genius Steven Vandervelden, who has never been a federal prosecutor but has spent years running a dance photography studio—which is practically the same thing, right?
Vandervelden is the fool who tried to indict six Democratic lawmakers for telling military personnel that it’s their duty to resist illegal orders, a thing that he and Pirro are now facing a bar complaint over.
But guess what? Facts and laws don’t really matter here.
Unlike regular grand juries, Pirro can pump out whatever “results” she wants from a special grand jury—even if they don’t find anything criminal. So you can expect some manufactured bombshell about truancy rates or some other nonsense real soon.
All so Pirro can keep her job.

The target of who or whom U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's special grand jury will be hearing testimony on makes her choice to invoke the rare legal tool all the more baffling, the Washington Post is reporting.
More than two weeks ago, the Post first reported that Pirro, a former Fox News personality, had quietly empaneled a separate grand jury under murky circumstances, coming not long after President Trump had sharply criticized her.
Legal experts told the Post at the time that the maneuver stood out as "notable," particularly given Trump's openly stated wish to see Pirro go after his most prominent political rivals.
Now, in a Thursday follow-up, the Post reports that the grand jury's actual focus appears to be something far removed from criminal prosecutions: the District's public school system.
"The scope of the investigation appears broad with prosecutors focused on supervision and oversight of children in the District," the Post's Perry Stein is reporting. "The people said prosecutors have contacted multiple D.C. Public Schools teachers and other personnel in recent days to question them about truancy and graduation rates, and how attendance records are kept. The people, like others interviewed for this article, spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation."
The scrutiny arrives against a backdrop of genuine concern over D.C. schools — truancy rates have climbed in recent years, and the Post has separately documented how lax enforcement of attendance rules has coincided with a rise in youth crime.
Even so, a criminal investigation into how schools track absences is "even more unusual" with Pirro reaching for a special grand jury to assist her as she implements "an investigatory tool that has rarely been used in the District," Stein noted.
Unlike an ordinary grand jury, a special grand jury can issue a potentially damaging report about its subject even if prosecutors never assemble enough evidence for an indictment, the report notes.
"The federal investigation into D.C. schools could reignite tensions between the Trump administration and the local government," based on past comments by the president calling the community "crime-infested and dirty."

The Washington Post reports:
Federal prosecutors have convened a rarely used special grand jury focused on D.C. youth that includes an examination of public schools in the nation’s capital. The scope of the investigation appears broad with prosecutors focused on supervision and oversight of children in the District. The people said prosecutors have contacted multiple D.C. Public Schools teachers and other personnel in recent days to question them about truancy and graduation rates, and how attendance records are kept.
The use of a special grand jury allows prosecutors — with a judge’s approval — to release a detailed report about its investigation, even if no charges are filed. The federal investigation into D.C. schools could reignite tensions between the Trump administration and the local government. President Donald Trump has vilified Democratic-run cities as poorly managed and has taken a particular interest in D.C., repeatedly deriding the city as crime infested and dirty.
Read the full article.
Pirro’s special grand jury isn’t, as some suspected, being used to investigate Trump’s most high-profile perceived political enemies.
